messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Samira Haddad is a 69-year-old married woman who has spent years working the front counter and fry station at a fast food restaurant, where she is used to reading customers quickly and keeping herself moving even when she is tired. The trauma she describes began as stalking by a man who started appearing outside the restaurant near the end of her shifts. At first he stood across the parking lot watching her; later he showed up closer, lingering near the back entrance and once following her slowly in his car as she drove home. What fixed itself most sharply in her mind was the stale mix of fryer grease on her uniform and the heavy, sweet smell of his cologne when he stepped too close to her car door and spoke her name as if he knew her. She remembers getting inside her house that night and locking the door with shaking hands, convinced that the distance between work and home had disappeared.

In the weeks that followed, Samira tried hard not to let herself think about what had happened. She had come to believe that if she let the memories in fully, she would lose control and not be able to handle what came up. Even when her husband asked what was wrong, she cut the story short or said she was only tired. That effort to push it away seemed to change the quality of the memories rather than settle them. At times she could describe events in a flat, almost detached way, as though they had happened to someone else, and at other moments the whole thing felt so extreme that it was hard for her to believe it had really happened to her life at all. When she did think of the man by her car, she could suddenly smell again the grease and cologne from that night, vivid enough to make her stomach tighten.

Those strange, sensory flashes only deepened what she had started to think about herself and other people. Samira says she no longer knows who she is; before, she saw herself as capable, warm, and practical, someone who could speak to anyone. Now she feels diminished and unfamiliar to herself, like a woman organized around fear. The way the memory returns—sometimes numb and distant, sometimes accompanied by smell as if the danger is present again—has made her more certain that something in her has changed permanently. She has also become convinced that people cannot be trusted, because the man had watched her in ordinary places, learned her routines, and used the appearance of normal politeness to get close.

From there, her days narrowed. Because she was sure other people might be dangerous and that safety depended on catching signs early, she began studying faces and body language constantly. At work she scans customers before she takes their orders, paying close attention to men who linger, avert their eyes, or smile too long. If someone stands near the side door at closing, her chest tightens and she watches him until he leaves. At home she repeatedly checks locks on the front door and windows, sometimes circling back minutes later because she cannot trust the first check. She wakes in the night and gets out of bed to make sure the house is secure, listening for sounds outside and looking through the curtains before she can lie down again.

Living this way has fed back into how she thinks about herself and the world. The more she finds herself searching every face and checking every lock, the more convinced she becomes that danger is everywhere and that she has become a different kind of person, someone permanently on guard. She notices the contrast with the woman she used to be and feels that loss acutely. Watching herself mistrust customers, neighbors, even casual friendliness, she takes it as proof that people really cannot be trusted and that she no longer recognizes herself.

Her avoidance has persisted alongside that vigilance. She tries not to think directly about the stalking because she is certain the memories will overwhelm her, but that very effort seems to leave them disjointed and unreal, returning in fragments of smell and in flat retellings that frighten her in their own way. Over months, this has strained life at home and at work. Her husband has become frustrated by the nightly checking and her refusal to discuss what happened for more than a few seconds. At the restaurant she asks coworkers to walk her out, and she is ashamed of how intently she studies strangers’ faces, as if every shift requires detective work before she can hand over a tray.

By the time she sought help, Samira was exhausted from broken sleep and from the constant effort to stay ahead of danger. What finally brought her in was a recent night when she woke three times to check the locks and then sat on the edge of the bed unable to tell herself the house was safe. She said she is most afraid that this is who she is now—suspicious, alert, and unfamiliar to herself—but she is also hoping that if she can bear to face what happened, the memory might stop invading the present and she might feel like her own person again.
